extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of logic, philosophy, and the theory of inference
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and principles for forming, analysing, and judging syllogisms and other forms of ratiocination, including treatment of singular propositions, quantification of predicates, numerical propositions, axiomatic foundations, and common fallacies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish definitions from statements of fact
rubrics_metrics.description: A definition (or part of a definition) is not the same as a factual premise; a definition's truth does not make the corresponding factual assertion true when the factual assertion purports to state existence or occurrence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'A dragon is a thing which breathes flame' used as a definition is not a factual claim that any real creature breathes flame. If one premise is a definition and another is a false factual statement, the real (factual) premise cannot be the definition. Treat predicates appearing in definitions differently from factual predication; do not count definitional containments as empirical support of existence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualify predicates for imaginary vs. real entities
rubrics_metrics.description: When a class-name includes imaginary as well as real instances, predicates about such instances must indicate the modality (e.g., 'imagined') rather than assert reality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If 'serpent' is taken to include imaginary serpents, one must not assert that an imaginary creature 'breathes flame' (which implies reality); instead predicate must be framed like 'imagined to breathe flame.' Example syllogism adjustment: conclusion should be 'Some serpents either do or are imagined to breathe flame.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid equivocation on terms with multiple senses
rubrics_metrics.description: Many philosophical and leading terms have innumerable shades of meaning; an argument may appear fallacious if critic and proponent use different senses of a term.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious before declaring an argument 'entirely upon words'—a sagacious mind may discern non-obvious links between senses that make an argument valid. Evaluate whether disputed terms are being used consistently in the same sense across premises and conclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Obversion and other equivalent propositional forms correctly
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain changes of expression (equivalent propositional forms) permit valid immediate inferences; one common transformation is Obversion (changing an affirmation into denial of its negative, and vice versa).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize permitted immediate transformations (per Bain and others) and apply them when deriving equivalent propositions; know the standard lists of equivalent forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classify oppositions (contraries, subtraries, contradictories, subalterns)
rubrics_metrics.description: Categorize propositions into logical oppositions for correct inference: contraries (All A is B / No A is B), subtraries (Some A is B / Some A is not B), contradictories (All A is B / Some A is not B; No A is B / Some A is B), and subalternate pairs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these oppositional relationships when testing consistency among categorical propositions and when performing conversions or reductions in syllogistic reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat singular propositions cautiously in syllogistic inference
rubrics_metrics.description: Singular propositions (e.g., 'Socrates is wise') are debated as to whether they are best classed with universals (Total) or treated separately; syllogisms formed from two singular premises may often be mere abbreviations or immediate inferences rather than genuine syllogistic advances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine whether predicates are part of the meaning of the singular name; if so, the 'inference' may only be restating connotations. Require that premises be 'real' and predicates not merely connoted by the subject for a singular-syllogism to count as genuine deduction. Examples: distinguishing between mere grammatical abbreviation and a true inferential step.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize the limited inference-content of conclusions relative to premises
rubrics_metrics.description: In every syllogism the conclusion contains less than is asserted in the two premises taken together; omission of the middle term may leave a conclusion that reproduces only part of the original assertion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware that deriving a conclusion by dropping parts of combined premises does not necessarily amount to a new intellectual advance; assess whether the omitted information constitutes a genuine inference or only a verbal reduction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider De Morgan's 'numerically definite propositions' where applicable
rubrics_metrics.description: When premises supply quantitative proportions (e.g., 'most Bs are Cs' with known percentages), one can deduce definite minimum overlaps between classes and thereby strengthen the definiteness of conclusions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use numerical proportions to compute guaranteed intersections (e.g., 60% and 70% overlap imply at least 30% common members). Note the author's caution that such numerically precise syllogisms are of limited practical use because most everyday reasoning lacks such numerical precision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be critical of the practical value of highly technical formal systems
rubrics_metrics.description: Technical extensions of syllogistic forms (De Morgan's calculus, Hamilton's quantification) are genuine logical contributions but may be of limited practical use for ordinary reasoning, which lacks numerical precision or explicit predicate-quantification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reserve study of complex formal systems for cases where propositions have the required numerical precision or where predicate-quantification is explicitly meaningful; otherwise, prefer analyses that track fallacies arising from ordinary language usage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantification of the predicate (Hamilton's doctrine) — understand implications
rubrics_metrics.description: Quantifying predicates (e.g., reading 'All A is B' as 'All A is some B') changes conversion rules and yields new syllogistic forms and canonical canons, potentially amplifying legitimate moods and leading to different figure analyses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize both the theoretical advantages (new tests of correctness, expanded moods) and the critique that such quantification may not reflect what is actually present in the speaker's mind; apply with caution and awareness of whether predicate-quantity is 'present to thought' in the case examined.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use an appropriate fundamental axiom for deductive reasoning (nota notae / 'mark of a mark')
rubrics_metrics.description: An alternative axiom to dictum de omni is proposed: the mark of a mark is a mark of the thing (i.e., if A is a mark of B and B is a mark of C, then A is a mark of C); this axiom highlights the condition that makes deductive application a genuine inference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply this axiom as the basis for deduction when the relation is of 'markhood' rather than mere class inclusion. Be mindful of criticisms (e.g., Bain) that it fails to handle partial coincidence and the necessity of limitations when the middle term is shared with other things.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for partial coincidence and limitation when transferring attributes
rubrics_metrics.description: When transferring predicates through a middle term, one must limit inferences because A may share B only in common with other things; axioms that ignore partial coincidence risk implying erroneous co-extensiveness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not infer co-extensiveness of A and C merely from A carrying B and B carrying C; analyze whether other things also carry the middle term and apply necessary limiting clauses to avoid overextension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assign figure-specific purposes to syllogistic forms
rubrics_metrics.description: Different syllogistic figures are suited to different explanatory or discovery tasks: first figure for discovery/proof of properties, second for discovery/proof of distinctions, third for instances and exceptions, fourth for discovery/exclusion of species of a genus (per Lambert and Bailey).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When selecting or assessing a syllogistic form, consider the cognitive/epistemic aim (discovering properties vs. distinguishing kinds vs. finding instances) and whether the chosen figure is appropriate to that aim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat major and minor premises as interpretive safeguards rather than ontological necessities
rubrics_metrics.description: Major and minor premises in syllogistic form typically serve to interpret, limit, and make explicit the kind of likeness between known and unknown cases; reasoning can, in a looser sense, proceed without formal major/minor expressions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the major to specify what kind of likeness to observed cases suffices for inference, and the minor to identify that likeness in the new case. Regard formal premises as precautions against error rather than as strict ontological prerequisites for all reasoning from particulars.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid misunderstandings about petitio principii in syllogisms
rubrics_metrics.description: An apparent petitio principii (the major including the conclusion) is often a linguistic/conventional misunderstanding: both major and minor are sometimes jointly justified by the same experiential grounds rather than one proving the other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When accused of circularity (e.g., 'All men are mortal' proving 'Socrates is mortal'), recognize that general and particular assertions may be simultaneous formulations of the same evidential basis; analyze the evidential grounds rather than relying on surface-form circularity charges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Express general propositions to reflect inductive reasoning (use 'Any' formulation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rendering general propositions in the form 'Any A is B' better manifests that inductive reasoning proceeds from particulars to particulars, with general propositions vouching for the legitimacy of such particular-to-particular inferences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When explicating or teaching inductive inference, prefer formulations that make the role of particulars explicit (e.g., 'The men A, B, C, etc., are so and so, therefore any man is so and so') to avoid suggesting that induction is proof by an already-complete universal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be careful not to reify attributes as numerically distinct per subject
rubrics_metrics.description: Reject the view that each individual's appearance of an attribute constitutes a distinct attribute (Spencer's objection); general attributes should be conceived as a single resemblance-type rather than countless numerically distinct qualities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When forming general terms, treat the attribute as the 'one in the many' (a single resemblance or type) so that general language remains meaningful and communicative; avoid analyses that would make general knowledge impossible by fracturing attributes into innumerable token-specific instances.
